items.followUp: Name the three types of cellular organization and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Identifies the three main types of cellular organization.
rubric.description: Names unicellular, colonial and multicellular organization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for all three types.

rubric.why: Shows how cells are organized in organisms.
rubric.description: Explains that organisms may consist of one cell, a colony of cells, or many specialized cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the organization accurately.

modelAnswer: Organisms show three types of cellular organization: unicellular, colonial and multicellular.
A unicellular organism consists of one cell; a colonial organism has cells living together in a group; a multicellular organism has many cells, often specialized for different functions.

items.followUp: Write the names of four multicellular organisms.

rubric.why: Two correct examples establish knowledge of unicellular organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct examples.

rubric.why: Completes the required set of four examples.
rubric.description: Gives two additional correct unicellular organisms, making four in total.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for four correct examples in total.

items.followUp: What is bioinformatics? Name one other interdisciplinary science.

rubric.why: Defines the interdisciplinary nature of these sciences.
rubric.description: States that interdisciplinary sciences combine knowledge or methods from different disciplines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Provides examples of branches formed by combining disciplines.
rubric.description: Names two interdisciplinary branches, such as biophysics and biochemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct branch names.

modelAnswer: Interdisciplinary sciences are formed by combining knowledge or methods from two or more scientific disciplines.

items.followUp: In an experiment testing the effect of light on plant growth, identify the experimental and controlled groups.

rubric.why: Identifies the group receiving the tested condition.
rubric.description: The experimental group receives the treatment or is exposed to the variable being tested.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the experimental-group distinction.

rubric.why: Identifies the comparison group that does not receive the tested treatment.
rubric.description: The controlled group is kept without the experimental treatment and is used for comparison.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the controlled-group distinction.

modelAnswer: The experimental group is exposed to the variable or treatment being tested.
The controlled group is not given that treatment and serves as a basis for comparison.

items.followUp: What is a biological observation, and how can it help identify a biological problem?

rubric.why: Identifying a biological problem begins with noticing or observing a biological phenomenon.
rubric.description: States that the problem is recognized through observation of an event, condition or phenomenon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking identification to observation.

rubric.why: The observation should lead to a definite problem to investigate.
rubric.description: Explains that the observed issue is stated clearly as a biological problem or question.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the problem clearly.

modelAnswer: A biological problem is identified by observing a biological phenomenon or condition that needs an explanation.
The observation is used to state a clear, specific problem or question for investigation.

items.followUp: What happens to an animal cell placed in a hypotonic solution?

rubric.why: Defines hypotonicity in relation to the cell or another solution.
rubric.description: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration (and higher water concentration) than the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relative concentration.

rubric.description: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration (and lower water concentration) than the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relative concentration.

modelAnswer: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration and a higher water concentration than the cell; water moves into the cell.
A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration and a lower water concentration than the cell; water moves out of the cell.
An isotonic solution has the same solute concentration as the cell, so there is no net movement of water.

items.followUp: What is the nucleoid, and in which cells is it found?

rubric.why: Locates the nucleoid in cells without a true nucleus.
rubric.description: States that the nucleoid is found in prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria.

rubric.why: Describes the nucleoid's contents and lack of a surrounding membrane.
rubric.description: Explains that it is the region containing the cell's DNA and is not enclosed by a membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an accurate description.

modelAnswer: The nucleoid is the region of a prokaryotic cell that contains its genetic material (DNA).
It is not surrounded by a nuclear membrane.

items.followUp: What does systematics study besides the naming and classification of organisms?

rubric.why: Taxonomy is concerned with identifying, naming and classifying organisms.
rubric.description: Defines taxonomy through identification, nomenclature and classification.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the role of taxonomy.

rubric.why: Systematics includes the study of diversity and relationships among organisms.
rubric.description: Distinguishes systematics by its study of organismal diversity and relationships, including evolutionary relationships.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the distinguishing feature of systematics.

modelAnswer: Taxonomy deals with the identification, naming (nomenclature) and classification of organisms.
Systematics is broader: it studies the diversity of organisms and their relationships, including evolutionary relationships.
